nodes.name: Auto CMD Error Status Register (Offset 03Ch) (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: This register reports Auto CMD12/CMD23 error conditions, including command timeout (no response within 64 SDCLK cycles), CRC errors, end bit errors, index errors, and command execution failures, with timeout errors taking precedence over other error status indicators.

extras.full_text:
Command Not Issued By Auto CMD12 Error
Setting this bit to 1 means CMD_wo_DAT is not executed due to an Auto CMD12 Error (D04-D01) in this register.
This bit is set to 0 when Auto CMD Error is generated by Auto CMD23.

Auto CMD Index Error

This bit is set if the Command Index error occurs in response to a command.

Auto CMD End Bit Error

This bit is set when detecting that the end bit of command response is 0.

Auto CMD CRC Error
This bit is set when detecting a CRC error in the command response.

Auto CMD Timeout Error
This bit is set if no response is returned within 64 SDCLK cycles from the end bit of command.
If this bit is set to1, the other error status bits (D04-D02) are meaningless.
technical_terms: Command Not Issued By Auto CMD12 Error

nodes.name: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The Write Transfer Active status bit (bit 08) in the Host Control 2 Register indicates whether a write data transfer is currently active in the Host Controller, being set after a write command's end bit and cleared after receiving CRC status of the final data block.

extras.full_text:
08 ROC Write Transfer Active
This status indicates a write transfer is active. If this bit is 0, it means no valid write data exists in the Host Controller. Refer to Section 3.12.4 for more details on the sequence of events.

This bit is set in either of the following cases:
(1) After the end bit of the write command.
(2) When write operation is restarted by writing a 1 to Continue Request in the Block Gap Control register.
This bit is cleared in either of the following cases:
(1) After getting the CRC status of the last data block as specified by the transfer count (Single and Multiple) In case of ADMA2, transfer count is designated by Descriptor Table.
(2) After getting the CRC status of any block where data transmission is about to be stopped by a Stop At Block Gap Request.

During a write transaction, a Block Gap Event interrupt is generated when this bit is changed to 0, as the result of the Stop At Block Gap Request being set. This status is useful for the Host Driver in determining non DAT line commands can be issued during write busy.

1 Transferring data
0 No valid data

nodes.name: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: The Host Control 2 Register at offset 03Eh contains reserved bits in positions 07-04, with no defined functionality assigned to these bit fields.

extras.full_text: 07-04 Rsvd Reserved

nodes.name: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) (Chunk 2)
nodes.description: The Re-Tuning Request bit (ROC) enables the Host Controller to signal the Host Driver to re-execute the tuning sequence when temperature drift shifts the data window, requiring sampling point recalibration; this bit auto-clears when Execute Tuning is set and only functions when using variable sampling clock mode.

extras.full_text:
03 ROC Re-Tuning Request
Host Controller may request Host Driver to execute re-tuning sequence by setting this bit when the data window is shifted by temperature drift and a tuned sampling point does not have a good margin to receive correct data.
This bit is cleared when a command is issued with setting Execute Tuning in the Host Control 2 register.
Changing of this bit from 0 to 1 generates Re-Tuning Event. Refer to Normal Interrupt Status registers for more detail.
This bit isn't set to 1 if Sampling Clock Select in the Host Control 2 register is set to 0 (using fixed sampling clock). Refer to Re-Tuning Modes in the Capabilities register for more detail.

1 Sampling clock needs re-tuning
0 Fixed or well tuned sampling clock

nodes.name: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) (Chunk 3)
nodes.description: The DAT Line Active bit (Offset 03Eh, bit 02) indicates active data transfers on the SD Bus, setting after read command end bits or continue requests, and clearing when transfers complete or block gap stops occur, generating Block Gap Event interrupts when transitioning from 1 to 0.

extras.full_text:
02 ROC DAT Line Active
This bit indicates whether one of the DAT line on SD Bus is in use.

(a) In the case of read transactions
This status indicates whether a read transfer is executing on the SD Bus. Changing this value from 1 to 0 generates a Block Gap Event interrupt in the Normal Interrupt Status register, as the result of the Stop At Block Gap Request being set. Refer to Section 3.12.3 for details on timing.

This bit shall be set in either of the following cases:
(1) After the end bit of the read command.
(2) When writing a 1 to Continue Request in the Block Gap Control register to restart a read transfer.
This bit shall be cleared in either of the following cases:

nodes.name: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) (Chunk 4)
nodes.description: The Buffer Read Enable flag is a read-only status bit in the Host Control 2 Register that indicates when valid data exists in the host-side buffer for non-DMA read transfers, transitioning from 0 to 1 when block data becomes available and generating a Buffer Read Ready interrupt.

extras.full_text:
Buffer Read Enable
This status is used for non-DMA read transfers.
The Host Controller may implement multiple buffers to transfer data efficiently. This read only flag indicates that valid data exists in the host side buffer. If this bit is 1, readable data exists in the buffer. A change of this bit from 1 to 0 occurs when all the block data is read from the buffer. A change of this bit from 0 to 1 occurs when block data is ready in the buffer and generates the Buffer Read Ready interrupt.

nodes.name: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) (Chunk 5)
nodes.description: The Buffer Write Enable is a read-only status flag in the Host Control 2 Register that indicates buffer availability for non-DMA write transfers, transitioning from 1 to 0 when block data is fully written and from 0 to 1 when new buffer space becomes available, triggering a Buffer Write Ready interrupt.

extras.full_text:
Buffer Write Enable
This status is used for non-DMA write transfers.
The Host Controller can implement multiple buffers to transfer data efficiently. This read only flag indicates if space is available for write data. If this bit is 1, data can be written to the buffer. A change of this bit from 1 to 0 occurs when all the block data is written to the buffer. A change of this bit from 0 to 1 occurs when top of block data can be written to the buffer and generates the Buffer Write Ready interrupt. The Host Controller should neither set Buffer Write Enable nor generate Buffer Write Ready Interrupt after the last block data is written to the Buffer Data Port Register.

nodes.name: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) (Chunk 6)
nodes.description: The Read Transfer Active bit in the Host Control 2 Register indicates ongoing read transfer status, setting to 1 after read command completion or restart, and clearing to 0 when data transfer completes via block length specification, ADMA2 descriptor, or block gap request, triggering a Transfer Complete interrupt.

extras.full_text:
Read Transfer Active
This status is used for detecting completion of a read transfer. Refer to Section 3.12.3 for sequence details.

This bit is set to 1 for either of the following conditions:
(1) After the end bit of the read command.
(2) When read operation is restarted by writing a 1 to Continue Request in the Block Gap Control register.

This bit is cleared to 0 for either of the following conditions::
(1) When the last data block as specified by block length is transferred to the System.
(2) In case of ADMA2, end of read operation is designated by Descriptor Table.
(3) When all valid data blocks in the Host Controller have been transferred to the System and no current block transfers are being sent as a result of the Stop At Block Gap Request being set to 1.

A Transfer Complete interrupt is generated when this bit changes to 0.

nodes.name: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) (Chunk 7)
nodes.description: The Preset Value Enable bit in Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) controls whether SDCLK frequency and driver strength are automatically selected by the Host Controller using Preset Value registers (bit=1) or manually configured by the Host Driver through Clock Control and Host Control 2 registers (bit=0).

extras.full_text:
Host Controller Version 3.00 supports this bit.
As the operating SDCLK frequency and I/O driver strength depend on the Host System implementation, it is difficult to determine these parameters in the Standard Host Driver. When Preset Value Enable is set, automatic SDCLK frequency generation and driver strength selection is performed without considering system specific conditions. This bit enables the functions defined in the Preset Value registers.

1
Automatic Selection by Preset Value are Enabled
0
SDCLK and Driver Strength are controlled by Host Driver

If this bit is set to 0, SDCLK Frequency Select, Clock Generator Select in the Clock Control register and Driver Strength Select in Host Control 2 register are set by Host Driver.
If this bit is set to 1, SDCLK Frequency Select, Clock Generator Select in the Clock Control register and Driver Strength Select in Host Control 2 register are set by Host Controller as specified in the Preset Value registers.

nodes.name: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) (Chunk 8)
nodes.description: This register bit enables asynchronous interrupt support in 4-bit SD mode, allowing the host driver to stop SDCLK during interrupt periods for power savings while the host controller continues to deliver card interrupts when the card supports asynchronous interrupts and DAT[1] interrupt is used.

extras.full_text:
This bit can be set to 1 if a card supports asynchronous interrupts and Asynchronous Interrupt Support is set to 1 in the Capabilities register. Asynchronous interrupt is effective when DAT[1] interrupt is used in 4-bit SD mode (and zero is set to Interrupt Pin Select in the Shared Bus Control register). If this bit is set to 1, the Host Driver can stop the SDCLK during asynchronous interrupt period to save power. During this period, the Host Controller continues to deliver the Card Interrupt to the host when it is asserted by the Card.

1
Enabled
0
Disabled

nodes.name: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) (Chunk 9)
nodes.description: The Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) configures slot voltage: removable card slots (Type 00b) default to 3.3V or fall back to 3.0V, while embedded device slots (Type 01b/11b) select one supported voltage bit for the VDDH host interface.

extras.full_text:
If a slot is for removable card (Slot Type = 00b), Host System can set Voltage Support 3.3V or 3.0V. Host Driver selects 3.3V in default. If 3.3V is not supported, 3.0V is selected.

If a slot is for embedded device (Slot Type = 01b or 11b), Host System can set one of Voltage Support bits for host interface voltage (VDDH).

nodes.name: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) (Chunk 10)
nodes.description: The Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) specifies the SD Clock's base frequency using either 6-bit mode (10-63MHz for versions 1.00/2.00) or 8-bit mode (10-255MHz for version 3.00), with 1MHz units. The Host Driver uses this value to calculate clock divider settings while ensuring frequency limits are not exceeded.

extras.full_text:
This value indicates the base (maximum) clock frequency for the SD Clock. Definition of this field depends on Host Controller Version.

(1) 6-bit Base Clock Frequency
This mode is supported by the Host Controller Version 1.00 and 2.00. Upper 2 bits are not effective and always 0. Unit values are 1MHz. The supported clock range is 10MHz to 63MHz.

(2) 8-bit Base Clock Frequency
This mode is supported by the Host Controller Version 3.00. Unit values are 1MHz. The supported clock range is 10MHz to 255MHz.

If the real frequency is 16.5MHz, the lager value shall be set 0001 0001b (17MHz) because the Host Driver use this value to calculate the clock divider value (Refer to the SDCLK Frequency Select in the Clock Control register.) and it shall not exceed upper limit of the SD Clock frequency. If these bits are all 0, the Host System has to get information via another method.

nodes.name: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) (Chunk 11)
nodes.description: This register bit indicates the time unit of the base clock frequency utilized for detecting Data Timeout Errors in the host controller.

extras.full_text: This bit shows the unit of base clock frequency used to detect Data Timeout Error.

extras.full_text: This bit shows the base clock frequency used to detect Data Timeout Error. The Timeout Clock Unit defines the unit of this field's value. Timeout Clock Unit =0 [KHz] unit: 1KHz to 63KHz Timeout Clock Unit =1 [MHz] unit: 1MHz to 63MHz

nodes.name: ADMA Error Status Register (Offset 054h) (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The ADMA Error Status Register captures the ADMA state machine status when an error interrupt occurs, storing the state in the ADMA Error States field while the ADMA System Address Register holds the address near the error descriptor, enabling the host driver to identify and recover from the specific error location.

extras.full_text:
When ADMA Error Interrupt is occurred, the ADMA Error States field in this register holds the ADMA state and the ADMA System Address Register holds the address around the error descriptor. For recovering the error, the Host Driver requires the ADMA state to identify the error descriptor address as follows:

ST_STOP: Previous location set in the ADMA System Address register is the error descriptor address
ST_FDS: Current location set in the ADMA System Address register is the error descriptor address
ST_CADR: This sate is never set because do not generate ADMA error in this state.
ST_TFR: Previous location set in the ADMA System Address register is the error descriptor address

nodes.name: ADMA Error Status Register (Offset 054h) (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: The ADMA Error Status Register (Offset 054h) specifies that hosts must use ACMD22 for write block verification due to potential unwritten data in the controller, and documents that ADMA Error Interrupts occur when invalid descriptors (Valid=0) are detected at ST_FDS state, allowing driver identification of invalid descriptors.

extras.full_text:
In case of write operation, the Host Driver should use ACMD22 to get the number of written block rather than using this information, since unwritten data may exist in the Host Controller.
The Host Controller generates the ADMA Error Interrupt when it detects invalid descriptor data (Valid=0) at the ST_FDS state. In this case, ADMA Error State indicates that an error occurs at ST_FDS state. The Host Driver may find that the Valid bit is not set in the error descriptor.

nodes.name: ADMA System Address Register (Offset 058h) (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The ADMA System Address Register (Offset 058h) stores the physical memory address of the descriptor table used by the Advanced DMA controller to perform data transfers between system memory and the host controller.

extras.full_text: This register contains the physical Descriptor address used for ADMA data transfer.

nodes.name: ADMA System Address Register (Offset 058h) (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: The ADMA System Address Register (Offset 058h) holds the byte address of the executing command in the Descriptor table, which must be programmed on 32-bit boundaries by the Host Driver. ADMA2 automatically increments this address when fetching descriptor lines and ignores the lower 2 bits, assuming them to be 00b.

extras.full_text: This register holds byte address of executing command of the Descriptor table. 32-bit Address Descriptor uses lower 32-bit of this register. At the start of ADMA, the Host Driver shall set start address of the Descriptor table. The ADMA increments this register address, which points to next line, when every fetching a Descriptor line. When the ADMA Error Interrupt is generated, this register shall hold valid Descriptor address depending on the ADMA state. The Host Driver shall program Descriptor Table on 32-bit boundary and set 32-bit boundary address to this register. ADMA2 ignores lower 2-bit of this register and assumes it to be 00b.

nodes.name: Preset Value Registers (Offset 06F-060h) (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: Preset Value Registers (offset 06F-060h) automatically configure SDCLK frequency, clock generator, and driver strength settings based on selected bus speed mode when Preset Value Enable is set. During initialization, the host driver must manually configure the clock preset value before enabling automatic preset functionality.

extras.full_text: Table 2-41 shows a set of preset values per card or device. One of the Preset Value registers (06Eh - 062h) is effective based on the Selected Bus Speed Mode. Table 2-42 defines the conditions to select one of Preset Value registers and Figure 2-36 defines fields of a Preset Value register. When Preset Value Enable in the Host Control 2 Register is set to 1, SDCLK Frequency Select and Clock Generator Select in the Clock Control Register, and Driver Strength Select in the Host Control 2 Register are automatically set based on the Selected Bus Speed Mode. This means the Host Driver needs not set these fields when preset is enabled. A Preset Value for Initialization (060h) is not selected by bus speed mode. Before starting the initialization sequence, the Host Driver needs to set a clock preset value to SDCLK Frequency Select in the Clock Control Register. Preset Value Enable can be set after initialization completed.

nodes.name: Shared Bus Control Register (Offset 0E0h) (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The Shared Bus Control Register (Offset 0E0h) is an optional register whose devices require host system-specific drivers rather than Standard Host Driver control, as shared bus configuration is host system-dependent.

extras.full_text: This register is optional. The devices on shared bus are not intended to be controlled by the Standard Host Driver. This is because shared bus configuration depends on a host system; the devices on shared bus may be controlled by a specific driver of a host system.

nodes.name: Shared Bus Control Register (Offset 0E0h) (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: The Shared Bus Control Register (Offset 0E0h) manages back-end power supply for up to 7 embedded devices through individual bit controls (D16-D22), independent of host interface voltage (VDDH). Power control is effective for memory devices in Sleep State supporting CMD14 and SDIO devices when IOEx is disabled.

extras.full_text:
Back-End Power Control

Each bit of this field controls back-end power supply for an embedded device. Host interface voltage (VDDH) is not controlled by this field. The number of devices supported is specified by Number of Clock Pins and a maximum of 7 devices can be controlled.

D16
Back-end Power Control for Device 1
D17
Back-end Power Control for Device 2
D18
Back-end Power Control for Device 3
D19
Back-end Power Control for Device 4
D20
Back-end Power Control for Device 5
D21
Back-end Power Control for Device 6
D22
Back-end Power Control for Device 7

The function of each bit is defined as follows:
0
Back-end Power is Off
1
Back-end Power is Supplied

Back-End power control is effective for embedded memory devices in the Sleep State that support the Sleep command (CMD14) to reduce power consumption and embedded SDIO devices when IOEx is set to 0.

nodes.name: Shared Bus Control Register (Offset 0E0h) (Chunk 2)
nodes.description: The Shared Bus Control Register (Offset 0E0h) Interrupt Pin Select field enables interrupt pin inputs through bit-coded values, where bits enable INT_A, INT_B, and INT_C respectively, with 000b designating interrupt detection by Interrupt Cycle and enabling unsupported pins having no effect.

extras.full_text:
Interrupt Pin Select

Interrupt pin inputs are enabled by this field. Enable of unsupported interrupt pin is meaningless.

000b
Interrupt is detected by Interrupt Cycle
xx1b
INT_A is Enabled
x1xb
INT_B is Enabled
1xxb
INT_C is Enabled

nodes.name: Slot Interrupt Status Register (Offset 0FCh) (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The Slot Interrupt Status Register (offset 0FCh) provides logical OR status bits for interrupt and wakeup signals across up to 8 slots, enabling the host driver to identify which slot generated an interrupt when multiple slots share a signal; the register resets to 00h on power-on or software reset.

extras.full_text: These status bits indicate the logical OR of Interrupt Signal and Wakeup Signal for each slot. A maximum of 8 slots can be defined. If one interrupt signal is associated with multiple slots, the Host Driver can know which interrupt is generated by reading these status bits. By a power on reset or by setting Software Reset For All, the interrupt signal shall be de-asserted and this status shall read 00h.

nodes.name: Host Controller Version Register (Offset 0FEh) (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The Host Controller Version Register at offset 0FEh contains two fields: a reserved vendor version number field not for host driver use, and a specification version field where upper and lower 4-bits indicate the Host Controller specification version number.

extras.full_text:
This status is reserved for the vendor version number. The Host Driver should not use this status.

This status indicates the Host Controller Spec. Version. The upper and lower 4-bits indicate the version.

nodes.name: SEQUENCE (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This section specifies sequence flow charts for Host Driver interrupt handling, where "Wait for interrupts" indicates the driver waits for specified interrupt assertions with timeout checking. Double-boxed steps reference previously defined flows that may include interrupts.

extras.full_text:
This section defines basic sequence flow chart divided into several sub sequences.

"Wait for interrupts" is used in the flow chart. This means the Host Driver waits until specified interrupts are asserted. If already asserted, then fall through that step in the flow chart. Timeout checking shall be always required to detect no interrupt generated but this is not described in the flow chart.

This specification uses the double box like Figure 3-1, (the step (1) in Figure 3-5 and the step (5) in Figure 3-25), It means that the other flows, which already are shown, shall be performed. Therefore, the interrupt may be included in the other flows.

nodes.name: SEQUENCE (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: The abort command recovers from SD Bus errors, where SDIO abort (CMD52) always returns a response, but memory abort (CMD12) response depends on card state; if CMD12 fails to respond, the host driver must verify successful abort by checking for "tran" state using CMD13.

extras.full_text:
Implementation Note:
Abort command is used to recover from SD Bus error. SDIO transaction abort using CMD52 returns response but in the case of memory transaction abort using CMD12, response returns depending on the memory card state. If no response returns after issue CMD12, the Host Driver should check card state using CMD13. If the state is "tran" in the CURRENT_STATE, consider CMD12 is successful.

nodes.name: SEQUENCE (Chunk 2)
nodes.description: This specification describes an error recovery sequence for SD Bus operations, noting that alternative implementation methods exist using interrupts or polling. When commands cannot be issued due to SD Bus errors, the sequence returns a "Non-recoverable" status, requiring the Host System to power cycle the bus and reinitialize both controller and card.

extras.full_text:
Implementation Note:
The following sequence is one possible error recovery flow. There may be another methods, sometimes using interrupts or polling. It can be possible to use another flows, based on Host System requirements.

In these error recovery sequences, return statuses for the next sequence. When the Host Controller cannot issue the next command due to SD Bus error, the error recovery sequences return "Non-recoverable" status. In this case, the Host System may cut off power to the SD Bus, and then power on SD Bus and initialize both the Host Controller and the SD card again.

nodes.name: SEQUENCE (Chunk 3)
nodes.description: When Stop At Block Gap Request is set during the last block transfer, the Host Controller rejects it and completes the transaction normally without generating a Block Gap Event Interrupt. The driver must clear the Stop At Block Gap Request after Transfer Complete Interrupt if Block Gap Event status remains unset.

extras.full_text: If the Stop At Block Gap Request is set to 1 during the last block transfer, the Host Controller shall not accept the Stop At Block Gap Request and stops the transaction normally. The Block Gap Event Interrupt is not generated. When the Transfer Complete Interrupt is generated, and if the Block Gap Event status is not set to 1, the driver shall clear the Stop At Block Gap Request.

nodes.name: SEQUENCE (Chunk 4)
nodes.description: This specification describes the data transfer restart sequence, where setting Continue Request to 1 releases Read Wait, activates DAT Line and Read Transfer statuses, and auto-clears the request. Transfer completion is determined by data length, clearing active statuses and generating Transfer Complete Interrupt after all valid data is read.

extras.full_text:
To restart a stopped data transfer, set the Continue Request to 1. (The Stop At Block Gap Request shall be set to 0.)
After accepting the Continue Request,
(1) Release Read Wait (if the data block can accept the next data.)
(2) Set the DAT Line Active status and the Read Transfer Active status
(3) The Continue Request is automatically cleared by (2).
The end of the read transfer is specified by data length.
(1) Clear the DAT Line Active status and do not generate the Block Gap Event Interrupt.
(2) After all valid data has been read (No valid read data remains in the Host Controller), clear the Read Transfer Active status and generate the Transfer Complete Interrupt.

nodes.name: SD Card Detection (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: SD card detection is enabled by configuring four interrupt bits in the Normal Interrupt Status Enable and Signal Enable registers: setting Card Insertion Status Enable, Card Insertion Signal Enable, Card Removal Status Enable, and Card Removal Signal Enable bits to 1.

extras.full_text:
The flow chart for detecting a SD card is shown in Figure 3-2. Each step is executed as follows:

To enable interrupt for card detection, write 1 to the following bits:

Card Insertion Status Enable in the Normal Interrupt Status Enable register
Card Insertion Signal Enable in the Normal Interrupt Signal Enable register
Card Removal Status Enable in the Normal Interrupt Status Enable register
Card Removal Signal Enable in the Normal Interrupt Signal Enable register

nodes.name: SD Clock Supply Sequence (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This specification defines the SD Clock supply sequence for SD cards, requiring clock frequency calculation from the Capabilities register, configuration of the Clock Control register's Internal Clock Enable and frequency settings, verification of clock stability, and finally enabling SD Clock before issuing commands or detecting interrupts.

extras.full_text:
The sequence for supplying SD Clock to a SD card is described in Figure 3-3. The clock shall be supplied to the card before either of the following actions is taken.
a) Issuing a SD command
b) Detect an interrupt from a SD card in 4-bit mode.

(1) Calculate a divisor to determine SD Clock frequency by reading Base Clock Frequency For SD Clock in the Capabilities register. If Base Clock Frequency For SD Clock is 00 0000b, the Host System shall provide this information to the Host Driver by another method.
(2) Set Internal Clock Enable and SDCLK Frequency Select in the Clock Control register in accordance with the calculated result of step (1).
(3) Check Internal Clock Stable in the Clock Control register. Repeat this step until Clock Stable is 1.
(4) Set SD Clock Enable in the Clock Control register to 1. Then, the Host Controller starts to supply the SD Clock.
technical_terms: Base Clock Frequency For SD Clock

nodes.name: SD Clock Stop Sequence (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The SD Clock Stop Sequence requires the Host Driver to set SD Clock Enable to 0 in the Clock Control register only when no SD transaction is active (Command Inhibit DAT and CMD bits are 0), after which the Host Controller ceases SD Clock supply.

extras.full_text:
The flow chart for stopping the SD Clock is shown in Figure 3-4. The Host Driver shall not stop the SD Clock when a SD transaction is occurring on the SD Bus -- namely, when either Command Inhibit (DAT) or Command Inhibit (CMD) in the Present State register is set to 1.

(1) Set SD Clock Enable in the Clock Control register to 0. Then, the Host Controller stops supplying the SD Clock.

nodes.name: SD Clock Frequency Change Sequence (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The SD Clock frequency change sequence consists of two steps as detailed in Figure 3-5: step (1) addresses active clock conditions (omitted when SD Clock is off, see Section 3.2.2), and step (2) covers the frequency change procedure (see Section 3.2.1).

extras.full_text: The sequence for changing SD Clock frequency is shown in Figure 3-5. When SD Clock is still off, step (1) is omitted. Please refer to Section 3.2.2 for details regarding step (1) and Section 3.2.1 for step (2).

nodes.name: SD Bus Power Control (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: Figure 3-6 describes the control sequence for managing power delivery to the SD Bus interface.

extras.full_text: The sequence for controlling the SD Bus Power is described in Figure 3-6.

nodes.name: Changing Bus Width (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This specification describes the five-step procedure for changing SD bus width, including masking card interrupts, disabling IENM in SDIO/combo cards via CMD52, switching card bus width using ACMD6 (SD Memory) or CCCR registers (SDIO), and configuring the Host Control register for 1-bit or 4-bit mode.

extras.full_text:
The sequence for changing bit mode on SD Bus is shown in Figure 3-7.

(1) Set Card Interrupt Status Enable in the Normal Interrupt Status Enable register to 0 for masking incorrect interrupts that may occur while changing the bus width.
(2) In case of SD memory only card, go to step (4). In case of other card, go to step (3).
(3) Set "IENM" of the CCCR in a SDIO or SD combo card to 0 by CMD52. Please refer to Section 3.7.1 for how to generate CMD52.
(4) Change the bus width mode for a SD card. SD Memory Card bus width is changed by ACMD6 and SDIO card bus width is changed by setting Bus Width of Bus Interface Control register in CCCR.
(5) In case of changing to 4-bit mode, set Data Transfer Width to 1 in the Host Control 1 register. In another case (1-bit mode), set this bit to 0.

nodes.name: Changing Bus Width (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: This specification details the final steps for changing bus width in SD cards: SD memory cards complete the process immediately, while SDIO and combo cards require enabling interrupt bits via CMD52 and status register configuration. Locked cards must be unlocked before any bus width changes.

extras.full_text:
(6) In case of SD memory only card, go to the 'End'. In case of other card, go to step (7).
(7) Set "IENM" of the CCCR in a SDIO or SD combo card to 1 by CMD52.
(8) Set Card Interrupt Status Enable in the Normal Interrupt Status Enable register to 1.

Note that if the card is locked, bus width cannot be changed. Unlock the card is required before changing bus width.

nodes.name: Timeout Setting on DAT Line (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The Host Driver must configure DAT line timeout detection before SD transactions by: (1) calculating a divisor from the Capabilities register's Timeout Clock Frequency and Unit fields, and (2) programming the Timeout Control register's Data Timeout Counter Value accordingly.

extras.full_text:
In order to detect timeout errors on DAT line, the Host Driver shall execute the following two steps before any SD transaction. For more information regarding SD transactions, refer to Section 3.7.2

(1) Calculate a divisor to detect timeout errors by reading Timeout Clock Frequency and Timeout Clock Unit in the Capabilities register. If Timeout Clock Frequency is 00 0000b, the Host System shall provide this information to the Host Driver by another method.
(2) Set Data Timeout Counter Value in the Timeout Control register in accordance with the value from step (1) above.

nodes.name: Card Initialization and Identification (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This section presents the initialization and card identification sequence protocol for three SD Memory Card capacity types: Standard Capacity (SDSC), High Capacity (SDHC), and Extended Capacity (SDXC), as illustrated in Figure 3-9.

extras.full_text: Figure 3-9 shows new initialization and card identification sequence for the Standard Capacity SD Memory Card (SDSC), the High Capacity SD Memory Card (SDHC) and the Extended Capacity SD Memory Card (SDXC).

nodes.name: Card Initialization and Identification (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: When Stop At Block Gap Request is set during the final block transfer, the Host Controller ignores it and completes the transaction normally without generating a Block Gap Event Interrupt; the driver must then clear the Stop At Block Gap Request upon receiving the Transfer Complete Interrupt.

extras.full_text: If the Stop At Block Gap Request is set to 1 during the last block transfer, the Host Controller shall not accept the Stop At Block Gap Request and terminates the transaction normally. The Block Gap Event Interrupt is not generated. When the Transfer Complete Interrupt is generated, and if the Block Gap Event Interrupt Status is not set to 1, the driver shall clear the Stop At Block Gap Request.

nodes.name: Card Initialization and Identification (Chunk 2)
nodes.description: This specification defines the protocol for resuming stopped data transfers by setting Continue Request to 1, which activates DAT Line and Write Transfer statuses. Transfer completion is determined by data length, clearing Write Transfer Active status and generating Transfer Complete Interrupt after busy signal release.

extras.full_text:
To restart a stopped data transfer, set the Continue Request to 1. (Stop At Block Gap Request shall be set to 0.)

After accepting the Continue Request:
(1) Set the DAT Line Active status and the Write Transfer Active Status
(2) The Continue Request is automatically cleared by (1).

The end of transfer is specified by data length.
(1) Clear the Write Transfer Active Status, and do not generate the Block Gap Event Interrupt
(2) After the busy signal is released, clear the DAT Line Active status and generates the Transfer Complete Interrupt.

nodes.name: Signal Voltage Switch Procedure (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The Signal Voltage Switch Procedure defines the protocol for transitioning SD card interface voltage levels between 3.3V and 1.8V signaling modes to enable higher-speed data transfer rates while maintaining backward compatibility with legacy devices.

extras.full_text: Signal Voltage Switch Procedure

nodes.name: Signal Voltage Switch Procedure (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: This specification defines the SD card signal voltage switch procedure from 3.3V to 1.8V, initiated by CMD11 after S18A flag detection. The 12-step sequence includes stopping the SD clock, verifying DAT line levels (0000b then 1111b), enabling the 1.8V regulator with specific timing delays, and error handling with initialization retry.

extras.full_text:
(1) If S18A of CMD5 or S18A of ACMD41 is set to 1, signal voltage switch is performed according to the following steps. Otherwise, exits from this procedure.
(2) Issue CMD11.
(3) Check response and if an error is detected, go to step (12)
(4) Stop providing SD clock to the card.
(5) Check DAT[3:0] level. If the level is 0000b, the card is ready to start voltage switch sequence. Otherwise, go to (12) to quit the sequence.
(6) Set 1.8V Signal Enable in the Host Control 2 register.
(7) Wait 5ms. 1.8V voltage regulator shall be stable within this period.
(8) If 1.8V Signal Enable is cleared by Host Controller, go to step (12).
(9) Provide SD Clock to the card again.
(10) Wait 1ms.
(11) Check DAT[3:0] level. If the level is 1111b, switch to 1.8V signal level is completed successfully. Otherwise, go to (12).
(12) If an error occurs during voltage switch procedure, stop providing the power to the card. In this case, Host Driver should retry initialization procedure by setting S18R to 0 at step (7) and (21) in Figure 3-9.

nodes.name: SD Transaction Generation (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This specification defines the 9-step procedure for SD card transaction generation, including configuring block size/count registers, setting argument and transfer mode parameters, issuing commands via the Command register, handling completion interrupts, and reading responses before proceeding to write (step 10) or read (step 14) operations.

extras.full_text:
(1) Set the value corresponding to the executed data byte length of one block to Block Size register.
(2) Set the value corresponding to the executed data block count to Block Count register in accordance with Table 2-8.
(3) Set the argument value to Argument 1 register.
(4) Set the value to the Transfer Mode register. The host driver determines Multi / Single Block Select, Block Count Enable, Data Transfer Direction, Auto CMD12 Enable and DMA Enable. Multi / Single Block Select and Block Count Enable are determined according to Table 2-8.
(5) Set the value to Command register.
Note: When writing the upper byte [3] of Command register, SD command is issued.
(6) Then, wait for the Command Complete Interrupt.
(7) Write 1 to the Command Complete in the Normal Interrupt Status register for clearing this bit.
(8) Read Response register and get necessary information of the issued command.
(9) In the case where this sequence is for write to a card, go to step (10). In case of read from a card, go to step (14).

nodes.name: SD Transaction Generation (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: This specification details the SD card transaction generation procedure, including interrupt-driven buffer write/read operations through the Buffer Data Port register, block transfer handling (single, multiple, or infinite), and transaction completion steps involving Normal Interrupt Status register manipulation and abort sequence execution.

extras.full_text:
(10) Then wait for Buffer Write Ready Interrupt.
(11) Write 1 to the Buffer Write Ready in the Normal Interrupt Status register for clearing this bit.
(12) Write block data (in according to the number of bytes specified at the step (1)) to Buffer Data Port register.
(13) Repeat until all blocks are sent and then go to step (18).
(14) Then wait for the Buffer Read Ready Interrupt.
(15) Write 1 to the Buffer Read Ready in the Normal Interrupt Status register for clearing this bit.
(16) Read block data (in according to the number of bytes specified at the step (1)) from the Buffer Data Port register.
(17) Repeat until all blocks are received and then go to step (18).
(18) If this sequence is for Single or Multiple Block Transfer, go to step (19). In case of Infinite Block Transfer, go to step (21).
(19) Wait for Transfer Complete Interrupt.
(20) Write 1 to the Transfer Complete in the Normal Interrupt Status register for clearing this bit.
(21) Perform the sequence for Abort Transaction in accordance with Section 3.8.
Note: Step (1) and Step (2) can be executed at same time. Step (4) and Step (5) can be executed at same time.

nodes.name: SD Transaction Generation (Chunk 2)
nodes.description: This specification defines SD transaction generation sequences, categorizing them into three types based on DAT line usage: no DAT line usage, DAT line for busy signals only, and DAT line for data transfer, with the first two grouped as non-data transactions and the third as data transactions.

extras.full_text:
This section describes the sequences how to generate and control various kinds of SD transactions. SD transactions are classified into three cases:
(1) Transactions that do not use the DAT line.
(2) Transactions that use the DAT line only for the busy signal.
(3) Transactions that use the DAT line for transferring data.

In this specification the first and the second case's transactions are classified as "Transaction Control without Data Transfer using DAT Line", the third case's transaction is classified as "Transaction Control with Data Transfer using DAT Line".
Refer to the latest SD Physical Layer Specification and SDIO Specification for more detail about SD commands specification.

nodes.name: Transaction Control without Data Transfer Using DAT Line (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This section details the command protocol sequences for SD cards operating without data transfer on the DAT line, specifically explaining the initiation sequence (Figure 3-11) and completion sequence (Figure 3-12) for SD Commands in transaction control mode.

extras.section_title: Transaction Control without Data Transfer Using DAT Line
extras.full_text: In this section, the sequence for how to issue SD Command and how to complete SD Command is explained. Figure 3-11 shows the sequence to issue a SD Command and Figure 3-12 shows the sequence to finalize a SD Command.

nodes.name: The Sequence to Issue a SD Command (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This section details the procedural sequence required to issue commands to an SD (Secure Digital) card, specifying the exact steps and timing for proper SD command transmission and execution.

extras.section_title: The Sequence to Issue a SD Command
extras.full_text: The sequence to issue the SD Command is detailed below.

nodes.name: The Sequence to Issue a SD Command (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: This specification defines a seven-step sequence for issuing SD commands: verify Command Inhibit (CMD) flag is cleared, check for busy signal and abort command conditions, verify Command Inhibit (DAT) if needed, write command argument to Argument 1 register, set Command register to trigger command execution, then perform command completion sequence.

extras.section_title: The Sequence to Issue a SD Command
extras.full_text:
(1) Check Command Inhibit (CMD) in the Present State register. Repeat this step until Command Inhibit (CMD) is 0. That is, when Command Inhibit (CMD) is 1, the Host Driver shall not issue a SD Command.
(2) If the Host Driver issues a SD Command with busy signal, go to step (3). If without busy signal, go to step (5).
(3) If the Host Driver issues an abort command, go to step (5). In the case of no abort command, go to step (4).
(4) Check Command Inhibit (DAT) in the Present State register. Repeat this step until Command Inhibit (DAT) is set to 0.
(5) Set the value of command argument to the Argument 1 register.
(6) Set the Command register.
Note: Writing the upper byte [3] in the Command register causes the host controller to issue a SD command to the SD card.
(7) Perform Command Completion Sequence in accordance with 3.7.1.2.

nodes.name: The Sequence to Finalize a Command (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: Figure 3-12 illustrates the sequence for finalizing SD commands, identifying potential errors that may occur during execution, including Command Index errors, End bit errors, CRC errors, and Timeout errors.

extras.section_title: The Sequence to Finalize a Command
extras.full_text: Figure 3-12 shows the sequence to finalize a SD Command. There is a possibility that some errors (Command Index/End bit/CRC/Timeout Error) occur during this sequence.

nodes.name: Transaction Control with Data Transfer Using DAT Line (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This specification describes a command execution flow for SD/MMC host controllers that waits for Command Complete interrupt, reads the response register, optionally waits for Transfer Complete interrupt if data transfer is involved, validates response data for errors, and returns appropriate status codes.

extras.section_title: Transaction Control with Data Transfer Using DAT Line
extras.full_text:
(1) Wait for the Command Complete Interrupt. If the Command Complete Interrupt has occurred, go to step (2).
(2) Write 1 to Command Complete in the Normal Interrupt Status register to clear this bit.
(3) Read the Response register and get necessary information of the issued command.
(4) Judge whether the command uses the Transfer Complete Interrupt or not. If it uses Transfer Complete, go to step (5). If not, go to step (7).
(5) Wait for the Transfer Complete Interrupt. If the Transfer Complete Interrupt has occurred, go to step (6).
(6) Write 1 to Transfer Complete in the Normal Interrupt Status register to clear this bit.
(7) Check for errors in Response Data. If there is no error, go to step (8). If there is an error, go to step (9).
(8) Return Status of "No Error".
(9) Return Status of "Response Contents Error".

nodes.name: Transaction Control with Data Transfer Using DAT Line (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: This specification defines host driver requirements for SD card data transfer operations: only non-busy commands should be issued during transfer completion waits, Auto CMD12 completion is monitored via Transfer Complete interrupt, and OUT_OF_RANGE errors should be ignored when reading the last block of unprotected memory areas using CMD18.

extras.section_title: Transaction Control with Data Transfer Using DAT Line
extras.full_text:
Note1: While waiting for the Transfer Complete interrupt, the Host Driver shall only issue commands that do not use the busy signal.
Note2: The Host Driver shall judge the Auto CMD12 complete by monitoring Transfer Complete.
Note3: When the last block of un-protected area is read using memory multiple block read command (CMD18), OUT_OF_RANGE error may occur even if the sequence is correct. The Host Driver should ignore it. This error will appear in the response of Auto CMD12 or in the response of the next memory command.

nodes.name: Transaction Control with Data Transfer Using DAT Line (Chunk 2)
nodes.description: This specification defines SD card data transfer methods via DAT line, distinguishing between DMA and non-DMA execution modes, and describing three transfer types: Single Block (one block), Multiple Block (one or more blocks), and Infinite Block (continues until abort command CMD12/CMD52).

extras.section_title: Transaction Control with Data Transfer Using DAT Line
extras.full_text:
Depending on whether DMA (optional) is used or not, there are two execution methods. The sequence not using DMA is shown in Figure 3-13 and the sequence using DMA is shown in Figure 3-14.

In addition, the sequences for SD transfers are classified into following three kinds according to how the number of blocks is specified:
(1) Single Block Transfer:
The number of blocks is specified to the Host Controller before the transfer. The number of blocks specified is always one.
(2) Multiple Block Transfer:
The number of blocks is specified to the Host Controller before the transfer. The number of blocks specified shall be one or more.
(3) Infinite Block Transfer:
The number of blocks is not specified to the Host Controller before the transfer. This transfer is continued until an abort transaction is executed. This abort transaction is performed by CMD12 in the case of a SD memory card, and by CMD52 in the case of a SDIO card.

nodes.name: Transaction Control with Data Transfer Using DAT Line (Chunk 3)
nodes.description: This specification describes a procedure for controlling SD card data transfer transactions using block gap interrupts, including steps for suspending and resuming transfers by monitoring Block Gap Event and Transfer Complete status bits, issuing suspend commands, and checking response data BS/BR values.

extras.section_title: Transaction Control with Data Transfer Using DAT Line
extras.full_text:
(1) Set Stop At Block Gap Request to 1 in the Block Gap Control register to stop the SD transaction.
(2) Wait for an Interrupt. If Block Gap Event is set to 0 and Transfer Complete is set to 1 in the Normal Interrupt Status register, go to step (8). If Block Gap Event is set to 1, go to step (3).
(3) Set Block Gap Event to 1 in the Normal Interrupt Status register to clear this bit.
(4) Wait for the Transfer Complete Interrupt.
(5) Issue the Suspend Command in accordance with Section 3.7.1.
(6) Check the BS value of the response data. If BS is 0, go to step (7). If BS is 1, go to step (10).
(7) Save the register (000h-00Dh).
(8) Set Transfer Complete to 1 in the Normal Interrupt Status register to clear this bit.
(9) Set Stop At Block Gap Request to 0 in the Block Gap Control register to clear this bit.
(10) Check the BR value of the response data. If BR is 1, go to step (11). If BR is 0, go to step (13).
(11) Issues the command to cancel the previous suspend command in accordance with Section 3.7.1 Transaction Control without Data Transfer Using DAT Line.
(12) Check the BS value of the response data. If BS is 0, go to step (7). If BS is 1, go to step (13).
(13) Set Transfer Complete to 1 in the Normal Interrupt Status register to clear this bit.
(14) Set Continue Request to 1 in the Block Gap Control register to continue the transaction. At the same time, write 0 to Stop At Block Gap Request to clear this bit.

nodes.description: This section describes the operational sequence for data transfer operations when Direct Memory Access (DMA) is not utilized, requiring manual CPU-controlled data movement instead of hardware-automated memory transfers.

nodes.name: Using SDMA (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The specification outlines the procedural sequence for implementing Space Division Multiple Access (SDMA), a wireless communication technique that enables multiple users to share the same frequency channel by utilizing spatial separation through directional antennas or beamforming.

extras.full_text: The sequence for using SDMA is shown below.

nodes.name: Using SDMA (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: This specification defines Auto CMD12 Error Recovery sequence handling for SDMA operations, covering four distinct error scenarios: errors in CMD_wo_DAT only (A), errors in both CMD_wo_DAT and SD transfer (B), errors in SD transfer only (C), and SD transfer errors without CMD_wo_DAT issuance (D).

extras.full_text:
The sequence for Auto CMD12 Error Recovery is shown in Figure 3-22. Following four cases A-D shall be covered.
A: An error occurred in CMD_wo_DAT, but not in the SD memory transfer.
B: An error occurred in CMD_wo_DAT, and also occurred in the SD memory transfer.
C: An error did not occur in CMD_wo_DAT, but an error occurred in the SD memory transfer.
D: CMD_wo_DAT was not issued, and an error occurred in the SD memory transfer.

nodes.name: Using SDMA (Chunk 2)
nodes.description: This specification details an SDMA error recovery procedure that checks the Auto CMD12 Not Executed status bit and, based on error type (recoverable vs. non-recoverable), executes a conditional CMD12 sequence with specific error handling for CMD line errors and busy timeout conditions.

extras.full_text:
(1) Check Auto CMD12 Not Executed in the Auto CMD Error Status register. If this bit is set to 1, go to step (2). If this bit is set to 0, go to step (6). In addition, the Host Driver shall define PCMD flag, which changes to 1 if Auto CMD12 Not Executed is set to 1.
(2) Wait for Error Interrupt Recovery for CMD_wo_DAT.
(3) Check "Return Status". In the case of "Non-recoverable Error", go to step (16). In the case of "Recoverable Error", go to step (4).
(4) Issue CMD12 in accordance with Section 3.7.1
(5) If the CMD line errors occur for the CMD12 (One of D03-00 is set in the Error Interrupt Status register), "Return Status" is "Non-recoverable Error" and go to step (16). If not CMD line error and busy timeout error occur (D04 is set in the Error Interrupt Status register), "Return Status" is "Recoverable Error" and go to step (11). Otherwise, "Return Status" is "No error" and go to step (17).

nodes.name: Using SDMA (Chunk 3)
nodes.description: This specification describes a software reset procedure for the CMD line in SDMA, involving setting and verifying the Software Reset register, issuing CMD12 command based on card state, checking return status for errors, and validating the Auto CMD Error Status register's Command Not Issued flag.

extras.full_text:
(6) Set Software Reset For CMD Line to 1 in the Software Reset register for software reset of the CMD line.
(7) Check Software Reset For CMD Line in the Software Reset register. If Software Reset For CMD Line is 0, go to step (8). If it is 1, go to step (7).
(8) Issue CMD12 according to Section 3.7.1. Acceptance of CMD12 depends on the state of the card. CMD12 may make the card to return to tran state. If the card is already in tran state, the card does not response to CMD12.
(9) Check "Return Status" for CMD12. If "Return Status" returns "Non-recoverable Error", go to step (16). In the case of "Recoverable Error" or "No error", go to step (10).
(10) Check the Command Not Issued By Auto CMD12 Error in the Auto CMD Error Status register. If this bit is 0, go to step (11). If it is 1, go to step (14).

nodes.name: Using SDMA (Chunk 4)
nodes.description: This specification describes a software reset procedure for the DAT line in SDMA, involving setting and polling the Software Reset For DAT Line bit in the Software Reset register, with conditional branching based on the PCMD flag status to determine subsequent reset steps.

extras.full_text:
(11) Set Software Reset For DAT Line to 1 in the Software Reset register for software reset of the DAT line.
(12) Check Software Reset For DAT Line in the Software Reset register. If Software Reset For DAT Line is 0, go to step (13). If it is 1, go to step (12).
(13) Check the PCMD flag. If PCMD is 1, go to step (18). If it is 0, go to step (19).
(14) Set Software Reset For DAT Line to 1 in the Software Reset register for software reset of the DAT line.
(15) Check Software Reset For DAT Line in the Software Reset register. If Software Reset For DAT Line is 0, go to step (20). If it is 1, go to step (15).

nodes.name: Using SDMA (Chunk 5)
nodes.description: This specification defines five SDMA error status return codes that indicate different combinations of errors in CMD_wo_DAT command operations and SD memory transfers, including non-recoverable errors and various permutations of command versus transfer failure states.

extras.full_text:
(16) Return Status of "Non-recoverable Error".
(17) Return Status that an error has occurred in CMD_wo_DAT, but not in the SD memory transfer.
(18) Return Status that an error has occurred in both CMD_wo_DAT, and the SD memory transfer.
(19) Return Status that an error has not occurred in CMD_wo_DAT, but has occurred in the SD memory transfer.
(20) Return Status that CMD_wo_DAT has not been issued, and an error has occurred in the SD memory transfer.

nodes.description: This section describes the operational sequence and procedural steps required to implement and utilize Advanced Direct Memory Access (ADMA) functionality in a system.

nodes.name: Abort Transaction (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: Abort transactions terminate infinite or multiple block transfers on SD memory cards (using CMD12) or SDIO cards (using CMD52), executed either asynchronously when Command Inhibit is clear or synchronously after stopping data transfer via the Block Gap Control register's Stop At Block Gap Request.

extras.full_text:
An abort transaction is performed by issuing CMD12 for a SD memory card and by issuing CMD52 for a SDIO card. There are two cases where the Host Driver needs to do an Abort Transaction. The first case is when the Host Driver stops Infinite Block Transfers. The second case is when the Host Driver stops transfers while a Multiple Block Transfer is executing.

There are two ways to issue an Abort Command. The first is an asynchronous abort. The second is a synchronous abort. In an asynchronous abort sequence, the Host Driver can issue an Abort Command at anytime unless Command Inhibit (CMD) in the Present State register is set to 1. In a synchronous abort, the Host Driver shall issue an Abort Command after the data transfer stopped by using Stop At Block Gap Request in the Block Gap Control register.

nodes.name: Asynchronous Abort (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The Asynchronous Abort sequence involves issuing an Abort Command, performing a software reset by setting both DAT and CMD line reset bits to 1, then polling the Software Reset register until both reset bits return to 0, indicating completion.

extras.full_text:
The sequence for Asynchronous Abort is shown in Figure 3-16.

(1) Issue Abort Command in accordance with Section 3.7.1
(2) Set both Software Reset For DAT Line and Software Reset For CMD Line to 1 in the Software Reset register to do software reset.
(3) Check Software Reset For DAT Line and Software Reset For CMD Line in the Software Reset register. If both Software Reset For DAT Line and Software Reset For CMD Line are 0, go to "End". If either Software Reset For DAT Line or Software Reset For CMD Line is 1, go to step (3).

nodes.name: Synchronous Abort (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This specification details the six-step synchronous abort procedure for SD transactions, which involves setting the Block Gap Control register, waiting for Transfer Complete Interrupt, issuing an Abort Command, performing software reset for DAT and CMD lines, and verifying reset completion before termination.

extras.full_text:
The sequence for Synchronous Abort is shown in Figure 3-17

(1) Set the Stop At Block Gap Request in the Block Gap Control register to 1 to stop SD transactions.
(2) Wait for the Transfer Complete Interrupt.
(3) Set the Transfer Complete to 1 in the Normal Interrupt Status register to clear this bit.
(4) Issue the Abort Command in accordance with Section 3.7.1
(5) Set both Software Reset For DAT Line and Software Reset For CMD Line to 1 in the Software Reset register to do software reset.
(6) Check both Software Reset For DAT Line and Software Reset For CMD Line in the Software Reset register. If both Software Reset For DAT Line and Software Reset For CMD Line are 0, go to 'End'. If either Software Reset For DAT Line or Software Reset For CMD Line is 1, go to step (6).

nodes.name: Changing Bus Speed Mode (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This section details the bus speed mode switching sequence for SD cards using CMD6 (memory) or CCCR register bits (SDIO), covering Default Speed, High Speed, and UHS-I modes. For Combo cards, the first switch method applies to both memory and IO functions, requiring card unlock before modification.

extras.full_text: This section describes the sequence for switching the bus speed mode; Default Speed, High Speed mode and UHS-I mode. The switch command (CMD6) is used to change memory card bus speed mode. The EHS bit (SDIO Version 2.00) or BSS[2:0] bits (SDIO Version 3.00) in the CCCR register is used to change the bus speed mode for SDIO card. In case of Combo card, either of the switch method changes both memory and IO bus speed mode. This means the first switch is effective. Refer to the Physical Layer Specification Version 3.0x and the SDIO Specification Version 3.00 for more information about switching bus speed. Figure 3-18 shows the sequence for switching bus speed mode for Combo Card. Note that if the card is locked, bus width cannot be changed. Unlock the card is required before changing bus width.

nodes.name: Changing Bus Speed Mode (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: This specification defines the four-step wakeup sequence from standby mode: waiting for a wakeup event, disabling and clearing wakeup event factors in control registers, enabling the SD clock, and configuring the SD bus width per Section 3.4.

extras.full_text:
The sequence for wakeup once in standby mode is shown in Figure 3-24.

(1) Wait for wakeup event.
(2) Set the enable bits of each wakeup event factor to 0 in the Wakeup Control register and then clear event statuses in the Normal Interrupt Status register. If necessary, set the Normal Interrupt Signal Enable register.
(3) Set SD Clock Enable to 1 in the Clock Control register.
(4) Set the SD Bus width in accordance with Section 3.4.

nodes.name: Error Recovery (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The Host Controller uses two interrupt status registers to handle errors: the Error Interrupt Status register for SD Bus transaction errors and the Normal Interrupt Status register for SDIO card function errors. SD Bus errors require recovery using abort commands before function error recovery, with the Host Driver saving and transferring error statuses to the Card Driver.

extras.full_text: Figure 3-19 shows concept of error report and its recovery. The Host Controller has 2 interrupt status registers. If an error occurs in the SD Bus transaction, one of the bits is set in the Error Interrupt Status register. If the function errors occur in the SDIO card, the card interrupt informs these function errors and the Card interrupt is set in the Normal Interrupt Status register. (The Card Interrupt is used to inform not only error statuses but also normal information. For example, to inform function ready.) The Card Driver shall do function error recovery because the Host Driver does not know how to control the function. In the case that function error occurs due to SD Bus error, SD Bus error recovery is required before function error recovery. Abort command is used to recover SD Bus, and then the Host Driver should save error statuses related to SD Bus errors before issuing abort command and transfer these statuses to the Card Driver. These statuses may be used to recover function error. Following explanations are related to SD Bus error recovery. This specification does not specify the function error recovery.

nodes.name: Error Recovery (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: This specification describes three host driver error recovery methods for SD cards when card driver recovery fails: using IOEx register toggling for SDIO function-level reset, issuing reset commands requiring re-initialization for memory/SDIO cards, or performing power-cycle reset with re-initialization.

extras.full_text:
Implementation Note:
If the Card Driver cannot recover the function errors, the Host Driver should try following methods.
(4) Using IOEx for SDIO card
IOEx may be used as the reset per function basis. Sequence is as follows:
Clear IOEx=0 and wait until IORx=0 and then set IOEx=1 again. SDIO may be recovered when IORx=1.
(5) Using reset command for memory and SDIO card
Re-initialization sequence is required.
(6) Off and on power supply for the SD Bus
The card may be recovered by the power on reset. Re-initialization sequence is required.

nodes.name: Error Recovery (Chunk 2)
nodes.description: The Host Driver implements Error Recovery sequences for two scenarios: (1) Error Interrupt Recovery triggered by the Error Interrupt Status register, and (2) Auto CMD12 Error Recovery with four classified cases, where memory write errors should utilize ACMD22 to retry unwritten blocks.

extras.full_text:
The two cases where the Host Driver needs the "Error Recovery" sequence are classified as follows:
(1) Error Interrupt Recovery:
If error interrupt is indicated by the Error Interrupt Status register, the Host Driver shall apply this sequence.
(2) Auto CMD12 Error Recovery:
If there are errors in Auto CMD12, the Host Driver shall apply this sequence. In terms of Return Status, Auto CMD12 Error Recovery is classified into 4 cases. It is shown in Figure 3-20. If error occurs during memory write transfer, strongly recommend using ACMD22 and then in the following recovery sequence, retry to send remaining blocks not written.

nodes.name: Error Interrupt Recovery (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: Error Interrupt Recovery follows a specific procedural sequence detailed in Figure 3-21, defining the steps required to detect, handle, and recover from error interrupts in the system.

extras.full_text: The sequence for Error Interrupt Recovery is shown in Figure 3-21.

nodes.name: Auto CMD12 Error Recovery (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: Auto CMD12 Error Recovery defines the procedure for handling errors that occur during automatic CMD12 command transmission in SD/MMC interfaces, specifying detection mechanisms and recovery protocols to ensure proper termination of multi-block data transfers.

nodes.name: Wakeup Control (Optional) (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This specification defines three optional wakeup events that can resume a Host System from standby mode: SD card interrupt (requires maintaining SD Bus power), SD card insertion, and SD card removal, with the preparation sequence detailed in Figure 3-23.

extras.full_text:
After the Host System goes into standby mode, the Host System can resume from standby via a wakeup event initiated by one of the following three events:

(1) Interrupt from a SD card:
If an SD card interrupt occurs, the Host System can resume from standby mode. If the Host System uses this wakeup factor, SD Bus power shall be kept on.
(2) Insertion of SD card:
If a SD card is inserted, the Host System can resume from standby mode.
(3) Removal of SD card:
If a SD card is removed, the Host System can resume from standby mode.

The sequence for preparing wakeup before the Host System goes into standby mode is shown in Figure 3-23.

nodes.name: Wakeup Control (Optional) (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: This specification defines the wakeup control configuration sequence for an SD host controller, requiring data transfer width and SD clock to be disabled, followed by clearing interrupt status registers and enabling specific wakeup event factors through the Wakeup Control and Normal Interrupt Status Enable registers.

extras.full_text:
(1) Set Data Transfer Width to 0 in the Host Control 1 register.
(2) Set SD Clock Enable to 0 in the Clock Control register.
(3) Clear the Normal Interrupt Status register and the Normal Interrupt Signal Enable register, and then set the enable bits of each wakeup event factor to 1 in the Wakeup Control register and set the bits of Normal Interrupt Status Enable register to use wakeup.

nodes.name: Suspend/Resume (Optional) (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: SD card suspend/resume functionality requires both the Host Controller and SD card to support "Read Wait" function, which can be initiated by the Host Controller. ADMA operation is incompatible with this feature.

extras.full_text: If a SD card supports suspend and resume functionality, then the Host Controller can initiate suspend and resume. It is necessary for both the Host Controller and the SD card to support the function of "Read Wait". ADMA operation does not support this function.

nodes.name: Suspend Sequence (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The suspend sequence procedure is illustrated in Figure 3-25, detailing the step-by-step process for transitioning the system into a suspended state.

extras.full_text: The sequence for suspend is shown in Figure 3-25.

nodes.name: Resume Sequence (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This specification defines a 5-step resume sequence procedure that includes restoring registers (000h-00Dh), issuing a Resume Command, checking the DF response value, and conditionally performing a software reset of the DAT line by manipulating the Software Reset register.

extras.full_text:
The sequence for resume is shown in Figure 3-26.

(1) Restore the register (000h-00Dh).
(2) Issue the Resume Command in accordance with Section 3.7.1.
(3) Check the DF value of the response data. If DF is 0, go to step (4). If DF is 1, go to 'End'.
(4) Set Software Reset For DAT Line to 1 in the Software Reset register for software reset of the DAT line.
(5) Check Software Reset For DAT Line in the Software Reset register. If Software Reset For DAT Line is 0, go to 'End'. If it is 1, go to step (5).

nodes.name: Read Transaction Wait / Continue Timing (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The Host Controller manages read wait operations at block gaps by coordinating DAT line activity and transfer states, while the Host Driver controls stop and continue requests. The Host Controller accepts Stop At Block Gap Requests only when positioned at a block gap with read wait capability enabled through Read Wait Control.

extras.full_text:
Implementation Note:
Read Wait, DAT Line Active and Read Transfer Active shall be set and cleared by the Host Controller.
Stop At Block Gap Request shall be set and cleared by the Host Driver.
Continue Request shall be set by the Host Driver and be cleared by the Host Controller.
Block Gap Event and Transfer Complete shall be set by the Host Controller and be cleared by the Host Driver.

The Host Controller can accept a Stop At Block Gap Request when all the following conditions are met.

(1) It is at the block gap.
(2) The Host Controller can assert read wait or it is already asserted.
(3) Read Wait Control is set to 1.

nodes.name: Read Transaction Wait / Continue Timing (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: The specification defines a three-step sequence for handling read transaction pauses: clearing DAT Line Active status upon stop request, clearing Read Transfer Active status after buffer completion, and clearing the Stop At Block Gap Request after transfer complete interrupt acknowledgment.

extras.full_text:
After accepting the Stop At Block Gap Request
(1) Clear DAT Line Active status and generate the Block Gap Event Interrupt
(2) After all valid data has been read (No valid read data remains in the Host Controller), clear the Read Transfer Active status and generate the Transfer Complete Interrupt.
(3) After accepting Transfer Complete Interrupt, clear the Stop At Block Gap Request

nodes.name: Write Transaction Wait / Continue Timing (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This specification defines the control responsibilities for write transaction gap handling, where the Host Controller manages DAT Line Active, Write Transfer Active, Continue Request clearing, and event generation, while the Host Driver manages Stop At Block Gap Request, Continue Request setting, and event clearing.

extras.full_text:
Implementation Note:
DAT Line Active and Write Transfer Active shall be set and cleared by the Host Controller.
Stop At Block Gap Request shall be set and cleared by the Host Driver.
Continue Request shall be set by the Host Driver and be cleared by the Host Controller.
Block Gap Event and Transfer Complete shall be set by the Host Controller and be cleared by the Host Driver.

nodes.name: Write Transaction Wait / Continue Timing (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: The Host Controller accepts a Stop At Block Gap Request only when two conditions are met: the controller is positioned at a block gap, and no valid write data remains buffered in the Host Controller.

extras.full_text:
The Host Controller can accept the Stop At Block Gap Request when matches all following conditions
(1) It is at the block gap.
(2) No valid write data remains in the Host Controller

nodes.name: Write Transaction Wait / Continue Timing (Chunk 2)
nodes.description: When a Stop At Block Gap Request is accepted during a write transaction, the system clears Write Transfer Active Status and generates a Block Gap Event Interrupt, then clears DAT Line Active status after busy signal release and generates Transfer Complete Interrupt, finally clearing the Stop At Block Gap Request.

extras.full_text:
After accepting the Stop At Block Gap Request
(1) Clear the Write Transfer Active Status and generate the Block Gap Event Interrupt
(2) After the busy signal is released, clear the DAT Line Active status and generate the Transfer Complete Interrupt.
(3) After accepting the Transfer Complete Interrupt, clear the Stop At Block Gap Request

nodes.name: PCI Configuration Register (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The PCI Configuration registers contain identification information required by the Host Driver to recognize the SD Host Controller on the PCI bus interface, with specifications detailed in Appendix A.

extras.full_text: As regards PCI bus interface, the Host Driver requires some information in the PCI Configuration registers to identify the SD Host Controller. It is specified in Appendix A of this specification.

nodes.name: Register Maps (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The PCI Configuration register enables Plug & Play and ACPI power management for PCI-based SD Host Controllers, with implementation details in Appendix A. Multiple SD slots (up to six) are supported through Base Address registers at offsets 10h-24h in the PCI Configuration Space Header.

extras.full_text:
The PCI Configuration register is a special register to support Plug & Play and ACPI power management. The PCI Configuration registers for the PCI Based SD Host Controller is defined as appendix A.

Multiple slots can be supported through the use of multiple Base Addresses within a single PCI Function. Each of these Base Addresses is configured through the Base Address registers at offsets 10h to 24h in the PCI Configuration Space Header. The PCI Specification allows for a PCI Function to have up to six Base Addresses. As such, a PCI Based SD Host Controller can support up to a total of six SD Slots.

nodes.name: Register Maps (Chunk 1)
nodes.description: PCI-based SD Host Controllers must allocate at least 256 bytes of memory address space per slot's Base Address register to access all specification-defined registers, with each slot using separate Base Addresses. Power Management registers report combined power consumption across all slots, and optional vendor-specific registers require an additional 256-byte area beyond standard registers.

extras.full_text:
A PCI Based SD Host Controller shall configure the Base Address register of each supported SD Slot such that it is a memory base address with at least 256 bytes allocated. This allows for enough memory address space in each Base Address to access all of the registers defined in this specification. Each set of the SD registers shall be implemented in a separate Base Address.

The values of Power Management register specified in the PCI Configuration registers should refer to the current and consumption values for all slots combined. It shall be read the total amount of power used by the PCI Based SD Host Controller, whether it has a single slot or multiple slots.

If Host Controller requires vendor specific register area, additional 256bytes area is added after the standard register area as shown Figure C- 2.

nodes.name: SD Controller Configuration Register MAP (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: The PCI configuration space for SD controllers is divided into three regions: standard PCI registers (00h-3Fh), SD Host Specification registers including Slot Information at 40h (40h-7Fh), and vendor-specific registers including Power Management capabilities (80h-FFh), with the Power Management register offset defined by the Capability Pointer.

extras.full_text:
PCI configuration space is divided into 3 areas.
00h - 3Fh : Registers defined in the PCI Bus Interface Specification
40h - 7Fh : Register area reserved for the SD Host Specification

Slot Information assigns to 40h and 41h-7Fh is reserved for future.
80h - FFh : Register area reserved for vendor unique registers

Implementation Note:
The Host Controller should place Power Management registers anywhere in the vendor unique register area. The offset address of Power Management register is set by Capability Pointer register. The Table C- 1 shows the case of offset being 80h (registers from 80h to 87h).

nodes.name: PCI Configuration Register (Chunk 0)
nodes.description: This section specifies PCI Configuration registers unique to PCI-based SD Host Controllers, while deferring to PCI Specification Version 2.3 for standard PCI Configuration register definitions.

extras.full_text: This section defines PCI Configuration registers that are specific for the PCI Based SD Host Controller. Refer to PCI Specification Version 2.3 for other standard PCI Configuration registers.

nodes.name: Base Address Register (Offset 10h) (Chunk 0)
